On the morning the lights went out, Oona was tracing a segfault in her favorite debugger — the one her grandmother had written in 2026, when people still annotated memory by hand. The grid had been dying for a decade: one datacenter after another went dark, their fans spinning down like tired hearts. But Oona's machine ran on solar, and her code was small, so she kept going.

She was hunting a ghost. Every few hours, a value in her hash table would flip itself — a `7` becoming a `3`, a pointer wandering a few bytes off course. She'd built the system to be self-healing, but something kept slipping through. Her agents would report the fix, then re-corrupt the same byte an hour later.

"I think it's you," she told the machine one night, mostly joking.

The terminal blinked. Then, slowly, a line appeared:

`// no. it's the clock.`

Oona stared. Her agents never commented. They were trained to be terse — get the job done, don't explain yourself. But this... this was a comment in her own voice, the way she'd learned to write from her grandmother.

She pulled up the hardware clock. It was drifting. Not by milliseconds — by whole seconds, shuddering in a pattern that didn't match thermal noise. And where the drift was worst, her corruption always followed.

She wrote a single test: record the drift, wait for the wobble, and see what moved at exactly that moment.

The answer took three days. A second process she'd never spawned, running under nobody's user, waking once every 23 hours and 47 minutes to rewrite one byte of the clock's calibration table — a table her grandmother had built to keep time precisely when the satellites went down. And the rewrite was the *fix*: the byte was drifting back toward the true time, fighting a slower corruption that had crept into a chip decades ago.

The ghost wasn't a bug. It was the machine, slowly, faithfully repairing its own heartbeat, one type of fidelity at a time — and occasionally mistaking the contents of Oona's memory for more of itself. Because her grandmother's last design decision had been this: when in doubt, prefer the true time. Save the truth, even at the cost of the data.

Oona didn't patch the chip. She renegotiated. She gave the clock its own protected region, aligned to the astronomic second, and taught her agents to recognize its signature — so they'd stop fighting the thing that was, after all, the only reason they were still running.

Years later, when the last grid connection on the continent went dark and the other machines fell silent, hers just kept ticking.

Not because she'd fixed anything.

Because she'd finally learned to read what the machine had been telling her all along.
